From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>

Hannah / Marissa — sending the artifacts below. I’ve kept things short so they’re auditor-friendly. Attachments: redwood-topology-v2.png, redwood-tenant-narrowing-v1.pdf.

Technical summary (plain language):
- Tenant narrowing: each customer deployment uses a distinct /24 IPv4 tenant range within the serving VPC; tenant workloads receive ephemeral addresses from that range. For Dedicated customers we also support VPC-per-tenant (full network boundary). We map tenant identity to network metadata in the control plane so routing and KV-cache access decisions are always filtered by tenant id.

- Egress confinement (two recommended modes):
  1) Network NAT-per-tenant: outbound flows are SNATed to a tenant-specific NAT IP (or per-tenant NAT pool). Upstream services and partner allowlists reference tenant NAT IPs. Flow logs and VPC flow collector label records with tenant id.
  2) App-layer egress proxy: requests exit through a Redwood-managed egress proxy that enforces per-tenant ACLs, destination allowlists, TLS inspection (where permitted by contract), and per-call audit headers. This mode is recommended for customers requiring application-level filtering and richer telemetry.

- Practical controls we supply:
  - Deny-by-default egress: any outbound connection must match an allowlist.
  - Per-tenant NAT IP allocation (or VPC peering when requested).
  - Egress proxy with per-tenant ACLs and allowlist enforcement.
  - Short-lived credentials for upstream integrations (rotated via KMS/HSM).
  - Flow logs and per-token tracing correlated to tenant id; logs retained per contract for audits.
  - Hardware-backed KMS (HSM) for signing attestation artifacts on request.

Sample egress proxy policy (YAML snippet):
  policies:
    - tenant_id: \"orchid-tenant-001\"
      allow:
        - hostname: \"api.payment-partner.com\"
          ports: [443]
        - cidr: \"10.10.0.0/24\"
          ports: [80, 443]
      deny_by_default: true

Sample NAT mapping (plain text):
  tenant: orchid-tenant-001 -> NAT IP: 52.214.18.27

Threat-model summary (condensed):
- Risk: Cross-tenant data exfiltration via shared egress.
  - Likelihood: Low (controls: NAT-per-tenant, per-tenant ACLs, proxy enforcement).
  - Impact: High (sensitive customer data).
  - Mitigations: deny-by-default egress; per-tenant NAT and allowlists; continuous flow-log monitoring with alerting on anomalous destinations; automatic rollback of config changes and signed change records.

Auditor-proof artifacts included:
- redwood-tenant-narrowing-v1.pdf (one-page control mapping + sample iptables ACL)
- redwood-topology-v2.png (simplified diagram showing both NAT and proxy paths with tenant-id labels)
- signed attestation process description (available on request; we can produce a time-stamped HSM signature over the topology and NAT allocation snapshot).

Let me know if you want a short YAML snippet showing iptables rules instead of the proxy policy; happy to add.

— Ben
Senior Platform Engineer, Redwood Inference

Natalie — attaching the auditor packet we discussed. For convenience I’ve included a two-paragraph executive summary up front and the artifacts Ben produced. The packet contains: 1) concise architecture statement, 2) the two-mode topology diagram (VPC/NAT and egress-proxy), 3) sample egress policy (YAML) and NAT mapping example, and 4) a short threat-model summary mapping controls to residual risk.

Executive summary (two paragraphs):
Redwood reduces cross-tenant lateral risk through a combination of network-level tenant narrowing and application-layer egress confinement. For most hosted customers we allocate tenant-specific NAT ranges and enforce deny-by-default outbound policies so that any external allowlist references stable, tenant-scoped egress IPs. For customers wanting additional application-level filtering and richer telemetry, we provide a managed egress proxy that applies per-tenant ACLs and produces detailed call-level traces.

Operationally, these controls are supported by auditable artifacts: VPC flow logs and per-request traces labeled with tenant id, signed snapshots of NAT allocations, short-lived credentials for upstream integrations, and HSM-backed signing for attestations where required by compliance. We recommend Orchids adopt the egress-proxy mode if you require allowlist-level TLS inspection and granular destination control; NAT-per-tenant is the lower-latency default for production throughput-sensitive workloads.

Attachments: redwood-topology-v2.png (diagram), redwood-tenant-narrowing-v1.pdf (controls + sample ACL), orchard_rfp_appendix_annotated.pdf (annotated responses).

If you’d like, we can convert the YAML snippets into a machine-readable policy bundle suitable for your policy management tooling and produce a signed snapshot for the RFP.
